vignette: A 27-year-old woman, three days into a chest infection, says her heart is racing. Temperature 38.4 °C. Lead II rhythm strip:
hints: Is there a P wave in front of every QRS?
Upright P before every beat, regular, about 120/min. Nothing fancy.
explanation: A regular narrow-complex rhythm at about 125/min with an upright P wave before every QRS and a constant PR interval. That is sinus rhythm, just fast. Fever, pain, dehydration, anaemia, anxiety, PE and thyrotoxicosis are the usual drivers; the real job is finding the cause.
features: Upright P wave before every QRS in lead II
pearl: Sinus tachycardia is a sign, not a diagnosis. A rate fixed at exactly 150/min should make you hunt for flutter waves instead.

vignette: A 71-year-old woman on a beta blocker and diltiazem has a routine ECG at her GP check-up. She feels fine.
hints: Measure from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS.
Every P conducts. The PR is long, but it never changes.
explanation: Every P wave is followed by a QRS, the rhythm is regular, and the PR interval is fixed at about 290 ms. A PR over 200 ms (one big square) with no dropped beats is first-degree AV block. AV-nodal drugs, like this combination, are a classic cause; so are high vagal tone in athletes and age-related conduction disease.
features: PR constant from beat to beat
Every P wave conducts: no dropped beats
pearl: One big square is 200 ms. If the PR is longer than one big square, it is first-degree block. It is really 'AV delay', not block: nothing is actually blocked.

vignette: A 22-year-old non-binary university rower has a pre-season ECG. They feel well; resting pulse is slow and a little irregular.
hints: Look at the PR interval, beat by beat.
The PR stretches, then one P wave stands alone with no QRS.
explanation: The PR interval lengthens with each beat (about 190, 290, then 340 ms) until a P wave fails to conduct; the cycle then resets with the shortest PR. That gives grouped beating. The block is usually in the AV node, so it is often benign in athletes, during sleep and with high vagal tone, though drugs and inferior MI can cause it too.
features: Then a non-conducted P wave (dropped QRS)
Shortest PR straight after the pause; grouped beating
pearl: Compare the PR just before and just after the dropped beat. Different: Wenckebach. Identical: think Mobitz II.

vignette: A 41-year-old Filipino man fainted overnight while sleeping off a fever of 39.5 °C. His uncle died suddenly in his sleep at 45.
hints: Focus on V1 and V2. Ignore everything else.
Coved ST elevation of at least 2 mm sloping straight into an inverted T wave.
explanation: Coved ST elevation of 2 mm or more in V1–V2, sloping down into inverted T waves, with a pseudo-RBBB terminal r′ and otherwise normal leads: the type 1 Brugada pattern, the only diagnostic type. Fever, some drugs and alcohol can unmask it. It is more common in men and in people of Southeast Asian heritage. Syncope plus a family history of sudden death are high-risk features.
features: Coved ST elevation ≥2 mm in V1–V2
ST slopes down into inverted T waves
r′ in V1, no reciprocal change, other leads normal
pearl: Recording V1–V2 one or two rib spaces higher increases the chance of catching a type 1 pattern.

vignette: A 31-year-old wheelchair basketballer in the national Paralympic squad has a routine pre-season ECG. She feels great.
hints: Count the big squares between beats. What's the rate?
Is there a normal P wave before every QRS?
explanation: A regular rhythm at about 46/min with a normal P wave before every QRS and a normal PR interval: sinus bradycardia. In trained athletes it is usually physiological, from high vagal tone and a big stroke volume. Other causes include beta blockers, hypothyroidism, sleep, raised intracranial pressure and sinus node disease.
features: Normal P before every QRS; PR about 170 ms
pearl: Rate shortcut: 300 ÷ number of big squares between R waves. About six and a half big squares here, so roughly 46/min.

vignette: A 63-year-old man with a heart attack two years ago has palpitations and feels light-headed. BP 92/60.
hints: Is the QRS narrow or broad?
Regular, broad, fast, and a scarred heart. Put it together.
explanation: A regular broad-complex tachycardia at about 175/min with identical QRS complexes. With a past MI, a broad-complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise. Clues to AV dissociation clinch it: P waves marching through at their own slower rate, and capture or fusion beats.
features: Broad QRS (about 165 ms), all the same shape
Dissociated P waves visible here and there
pearl: Assume any broad-complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise. After a previous MI, the vast majority are.

vignette: A 70-year-old woman with COPD has felt 'fluttery' and short of breath since yesterday.
hints: Ignore the QRS complexes. Look at the baseline between them.
A regular sawtooth at about 300/min.
explanation: Regular sawtooth flutter waves at about 300/min, with the AV node letting through every 2nd to 4th wave. The changing ratio makes the ventricular rhythm irregular, which can fool you into calling AF, but the atrial activity itself is perfectly regular and organised.
features: Sawtooth F waves at about 300/min (one per big square)
pearl: Flutter waves arrive once every big square (200 ms = 300/min). An organised, regular baseline means flutter, even when the QRS rhythm is irregular.

vignette: A 79-year-old woman has had two blackouts this week, one while sitting watching TV.
hints: Compare the PR before and after the dropped beat.
The PR never changes. A P wave just suddenly fails to conduct.
explanation: Regular P waves with a fixed PR interval, then a P wave suddenly fails to conduct (here 4:3). The broad QRS (bundle branch block) fits disease below the AV node. Mobitz II can progress to complete heart block without warning, which is why the blackouts matter.
features: Constant PR (about 180 ms) in conducted beats
Sudden non-conducted P wave; broad QRS
pearl: Mobitz I: PR stretches, then drops (usually the AV node, often benign). Mobitz II: PR fixed, then drops (usually below the node, high risk).

vignette: A 72-year-old woman with heart failure has a pre-op ECG before cataract surgery. No chest pain.
hints: Check the QRS width first. Then which way does V1 point?
Broad and deep in V1, broad notched R in V6, no small septal q waves.
explanation: QRS of 120 ms or more (here about 150), a deep broad QS in V1–V3, broad notched 'M-shaped' R waves in I, aVL, V5 and V6, and no septal q waves. The ST-T changes are discordant, pointing opposite to the QRS; that is expected in LBBB and is not ischaemia on its own.
features: Broad notched R in I, aVL, V5–V6; no septal q
pearl: WiLLiaM MaRRoW: W in V1 and M in V6 is LBBB; M in V1 and W in V6 is RBBB. LBBB hides ischaemia; the Sgarbossa criteria help in the right setting.

vignette: A 26-year-old man has had sharp chest pain for two days, worse lying flat and better leaning forward. He had a cold last week.
hints: Which coronary territory is the ST elevation in? All of them?
Look just before each QRS, and then at aVR.
explanation: Widespread concave ST elevation across several coronary territories (I, II, aVF, V2–V6), PR-segment depression, and the mirror image in aVR: ST depression with PR elevation. No reciprocal ST depression elsewhere. Sinus tachycardia is common, and pain that eases on leaning forward fits.
features: Diffuse concave ST elevation, not confined to one territory
aVR: ST depression with PR elevation
No reciprocal change except aVR and V1
pearl: PR elevation in aVR is the quiet tell of pericarditis. An ST/T ratio over 0.25 in V6 favours pericarditis over early repolarisation.

vignette: A 19-year-old woman felt her heart start pounding suddenly while bending to tie her shoelaces. She is otherwise well.
hints: Narrow or broad? Regular or irregular?
Regular, narrow, very fast, no visible P waves, sudden onset.
explanation: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at about 185/min with no visible P waves (they are buried in or just after the QRS). Sudden onset and offset in a young, well person fits AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia, the commonest regular SVT, and one that is more common in women.
features: No P waves visible before the QRS
pearl: In AVNRT, look for a 'pseudo-r′' in V1 or 'pseudo-S' in the inferior leads: the retrograde P wave hiding at the end of the QRS.

vignette: A 48-year-old woman notices 'skipped beats' after her third coffee of the morning.
hints: Look at every second beat: early, broad, and no P wave in front.
Broad complex with a T wave pointing the opposite way, then a pause.
explanation: Every second beat is a premature, broad, bizarre QRS with no P wave before it and a T wave pointing the opposite way, followed by a full compensatory pause: ventricular bigeminy. In a structurally normal heart it is usually benign. Caffeine, alcohol, stress, low potassium or magnesium, and structural heart disease are the usual suspects.
features: PVC: early, broad (about 150 ms), no P wave
Discordant T wave and full compensatory pause
pearl: Full compensatory pause: the sinus beat after a PVC lands exactly two cycles after the one before it, because the sinus node never noticed the PVC.

vignette: An 82-year-old woman feels exhausted and dizzy. Pulse 38 and regular.
hints: Mark the P waves and march them out. Then do the same for the QRSs.
P waves and QRS complexes each keep their own regular rate and ignore each other.
explanation: P waves march through regularly at about 88/min, broad QRS complexes march at about 38/min, and the PR interval is random because nothing conducts. That is complete (third-degree) heart block with a ventricular escape rhythm. A narrow escape would suggest a higher, junctional escape, which is faster and more reliable.
features: Broad escape QRS regular at about 38/min
No consistent PR: complete AV dissociation
P waves hide in QRS and T waves
pearl: In complete heart block the atria beat faster than the ventricles. If the ventricles are faster, think of another cause of AV dissociation, such as VT.

vignette: A 69-year-old man on digoxin and a beta blocker feels tired. Pulse 48 and regular.
options: Atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response
hints: Where is the P wave? Before the QRS, inside it, or after it?
Narrow QRS at 40–60/min with small inverted P waves just after it.
explanation: A regular narrow-complex rhythm at about 48/min with no P wave before the QRS; small inverted (retrograde) P waves sit just after it. The AV junction has taken over as pacemaker, at its intrinsic rate of 40–60/min, because the sinus node has slowed, here most likely from the drugs.
features: No P before the QRS; retrograde inverted P just after
pearl: Escape rates: sinus 60–100, junction 40–60, ventricle 20–40. Narrow at 40–60 is junctional; broad at 20–40 is ventricular.

vignette: A 58-year-old woman has a routine ECG for a new job. She is well, with no symptoms.
hints: Check the QRS width first. Then look at the shape in V1.
'Rabbit ears' rSR′ in V1, broad slurred S in I and V6.
explanation: QRS of 120 ms or more (here about 140) with an rSR′ 'M' in V1–V2, wide slurred S waves in I, aVL and V5–V6, and secondary T inversion in V1–V2. The right ventricle depolarises late, adding a terminal rightward wave. RBBB can be a normal finding, or reflect right heart strain (such as PE), ischaemia or congenital heart disease (such as an ASD).
features: Wide slurred S in I, aVL, V5–V6
pearl: Unlike LBBB, RBBB doesn't hide a STEMI: the start of the QRS is normal, so ST elevation stays readable.

vignette: A 54-year-old Aboriginal man presents to a remote clinic in the Northern Territory with an hour of crushing central chest pain.
hints: Which leads, and which artery supplies them?
Convex ST elevation V1–V4, lost R waves, and inferior reciprocal depression.
explanation: ST elevation from V1 to V5 (maximal in V2–V3) with hyperacute T waves and loss of R waves, plus ST elevation in I and aVL and reciprocal depression in III and aVF: an anterolateral STEMI from a proximal left anterior descending (LAD) occlusion. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people carry a higher burden of coronary disease and present younger, so chest pain at 54 gets taken seriously.
features: Loss of R waves in V2–V3
ST elevation in I and aVL
Reciprocal ST depression in III and aVF
pearl: ST elevation in aVL with inferior ST depression points to a proximal LAD occlusion, so a bigger territory is at risk.

vignette: A 66-year-old woman with diabetes has had two hours of upper abdominal discomfort and breathlessness. 'Just indigestion,' she says.
hints: The depression is horizontal and the T waves stay upright. Odd for ischaemia.
Mirror V1–V3 in your head: picture the back wall of the heart.
explanation: Horizontal ST depression in V1–V3 with upright T waves and a tall, broad R wave in V2 (R/S over 1). The anterior leads view the back of the heart from the front, so a posterior STEMI shows up upside down. Posterior leads V7–V9 would show ST elevation. It is a STEMI equivalent. Women and people with diabetes more often present without classic chest pain.
pearl: Flip the ECG over and hold it up to the light: the V1–V3 changes turn into Q waves and ST elevation.

vignette: A 57-year-old man collapses at a footy club barbecue. Bystanders start CPR; compressions pause while the AED analyses the rhythm.
hints: Can you find a single organised QRS complex?
Chaotic, irregular waves of changing size. No P, no QRS, no T.
explanation: Chaotic, irregular deflections of varying size and shape with no identifiable P waves, QRS complexes or T waves: ventricular fibrillation. It is a shockable cardiac arrest rhythm, which is exactly why early bystander CPR and a nearby AED save lives.
pearl: Coarse VF fades to fine VF, then asystole, over minutes. Survival drops by roughly 10% for every minute without CPR and defibrillation. Learn CPR.

vignette: A 17-year-old high-school runner has a sports ECG. The machine flagged 'irregular rhythm' and her mum is worried.
hints: Is there an identical P wave before every QRS?
The rate speeds up and slows down smoothly, in a cycle. Like breathing.
explanation: Every QRS has an identical upright P wave and a constant PR, but the rate drifts faster and slower in a smooth, repeating cycle. That is sinus arrhythmia: heart rate rises when breathing in and falls when breathing out. It is normal, especially in young, fit people.
features: Identical P waves before every QRS
R-R intervals vary smoothly and cyclically
pearl: Healthy hearts are not metronomes. Loss of sinus arrhythmia with age or diabetes reflects reduced vagal tone.

vignette: A 76-year-old woman admitted with a severe COPD flare is breathless on the ward. The monitor alarms for an irregular tachycardia.
hints: There ARE P waves. Do they all look the same?
At least three P-wave shapes, varying PR, irregular, over 100/min.
explanation: An irregular narrow-complex tachycardia at about 115/min with a P wave before every QRS, but the P waves come in at least three shapes and the PR interval keeps changing. That is multifocal atrial tachycardia, typically seen with severe lung disease, and it usually settles as the underlying illness does.
features: Three or more distinct P-wave shapes
pearl: The same picture under 100/min is called a wandering atrial pacemaker.

vignette: A 23-year-old woman has had episodes of sudden fast palpitations since her teens. This ECG is between episodes.
hints: Measure the PR interval. Short or long?
Look at the very start of the QRS: a slurred, ramp-like upstroke.
explanation: A short PR (under 120 ms), a slurred delta wave at the start of a broad QRS, and secondary ST-T changes: ventricular pre-excitation through an accessory pathway, the Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern. With symptomatic tachycardias it becomes WPW syndrome. A dominant R in V1 suggests a left-sided pathway, and negative delta waves in III can mimic inferior Q waves.
features: Dominant R in V1; pseudo-Q in III
pearl: AF in WPW looks like an irregular, very fast broad-complex tachycardia. It is dangerous because the accessory pathway has no 'speed limit' like the AV node.

vignette: A 19-year-old woman fainted the moment her alarm clock went off this morning. Her brother died suddenly and unexpectedly at 24.
hints: Measure from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave.
The T wave ends well past halfway to the next QRS, and it's notched.
explanation: QTc about 590 ms (normal is under about 460 ms in women and 450 ms in men), with broad, notched T waves. Syncope triggered by a sudden noise plus a family history of sudden death fits congenital long QT syndrome, classically type 2 (notched T waves, startle or auditory triggers). It predisposes to torsades de pointes.
features: QT about 590 ms at 60/min (QTc about 590 ms)
T wave ends beyond the R-R midpoint
pearl: Triggers by type: LQT1 exercise and swimming, LQT2 sudden noise or emotion, LQT3 rest and sleep.

vignette: A 70-year-old woman is rescued after a fall on an overnight bushwalk in the Tasmanian highlands. Core temperature 30.5 °C; she is shivering.
hints: Note the fuzzy baseline and slow rate. Then look right after each QRS.
A dome-shaped hump at the J point, biggest in V3–V6.
explanation: Sinus bradycardia at about 42/min, a long QT, shivering artefact, and a positive hump at the J point (Osborn or J waves), most prominent in the mid and lateral chest leads. J waves grow as core temperature falls, and AF and ventricular arrhythmias become more likely as hypothermia deepens.
features: Osborn (J) waves at the end of the QRS
pearl: Osborn waves are not unique to cold: hypercalcaemia, brain injury and subarachnoid haemorrhage can produce them too.

vignette: An 84-year-old woman with a pacemaker attends her routine device check. She feels well.
hints: Look for very sharp, thin vertical lines.
Two spikes per beat: one before the P wave, one before a broad QRS.
explanation: Sharp pacing spikes come before both the P waves (atrial pacing) and the broad QRS complexes (ventricular pacing) at a steady 70/min: dual-chamber pacing. Pacing from the right ventricle gives a broad, LBBB-like QRS with discordant T waves, so it is neither LBBB nor VT.
features: Atrial spike, then a P wave
Ventricular spike, then a broad QRS
Regular at the programmed rate, about 70/min
pearl: Right ventricular apical pacing gives an LBBB-like QRS with a superior axis, so the QRS is negative in II, III and aVF.

vignette: A 38-year-old woman notices occasional 'thuds' in her chest when lying in bed at night.
hints: Find the early beats. Is their QRS narrow or broad?
Early narrow beats with an odd-looking P wave in front.
explanation: Sinus rhythm interrupted by early beats with a differently shaped (here inverted) P wave and a normal narrow QRS, followed by a pause that is not fully compensatory because the ectopic resets the sinus node. Premature atrial complexes are very common and usually harmless; caffeine, alcohol, stress and poor sleep are classic triggers.
features: Early beat with an abnormal P wave
Narrow QRS, same shape as the sinus beats
pearl: PVC: broad, no P wave, full compensatory pause. PAC: narrow, odd P wave, non-compensatory pause.

vignette: A 61-year-old man's heart has been 'just racing' since this morning. The monitor shows a rate stuck at 150.
hints: What's the exact rate? Is that a suspicious number?
Look between the QRS complexes for a second wave hiding in the T.
explanation: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at almost exactly 150/min, with flutter waves at 300/min: one F wave shows between the QRS complexes and the next hides in the QRS and T wave. Atrial flutter with 2:1 block is easily mistaken for sinus tachycardia or SVT.
features: Every second F wave buried in the QRS or T
pearl: Any regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150/min is flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise.

vignette: A 74-year-old woman reports brief light-headed spells. This strip catches one.
hints: During the gap, is there a P wave that failed to conduct?
No P wave at all, and the gap isn't a multiple of the normal P-P.
explanation: Normal sinus beats, then a gap of about 3 seconds with no P wave and no QRS, then sinus rhythm resumes. There is no non-conducted P wave, so this is not AV block: the sinus node itself paused. Recurrent symptomatic pauses point to sick sinus syndrome (sinus node dysfunction), common in older people.
features: No P wave during the pause
Pause not an exact multiple of the P-P interval
pearl: Pause an exact multiple of P-P: sinoatrial exit block. Not a multiple: sinus arrest. A P wave hiding in the preceding T: blocked PAC, the commonest cause of a pause.

vignette: A 60-year-old woman with long-standing high blood pressure has become breathless walking uphill.
hints: Measure: S wave in V1 plus R wave in V5.
Huge voltages, with asymmetric T inversion in the lateral leads.
explanation: Very tall R waves in V5–V6, I and aVL with deep S waves in V1–V2 (S in V1 + R in V5 about 47 mm; Sokolow-Lyon criterion is 35 mm or more), plus downsloping ST depression and asymmetric T inversion in the lateral leads (the 'strain' pattern) and mild discordant ST elevation in V1–V3. Long-standing hypertension is the usual cause; aortic stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are others.
features: S V1 + R V5 about 47 mm (≥35 mm)
Lateral downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T inversion
pearl: Voltage criteria are insensitive, and young, slim people can exceed them without LVH. Strain changes make true LVH much more likely.

vignette: A 45-year-old woman has had three weeks of vomiting and diarrhoea and now has muscle cramps and weakness.
hints: What's that extra hump after each T wave?
Flat T waves, prominent U waves, mild ST depression.
explanation: Flattened T waves, prominent U waves (biggest in V2–V3, here taller than the T), mild ST depression and a long apparent QT that is really a QU interval: classic hypokalaemia. Vomiting and diarrhoea are common causes; diuretics are another. Low magnesium often comes along too.
features: Prominent U waves in V2–V3, taller than the T
pearl: In hypokalaemia, the T falls and the U rises. Mistaking the U for the T gives a falsely long QT.

vignette: A 49-year-old woman has had 30 minutes of crushing chest pain that started while shovelling soil. She is still in pain.
hints: No ST elevation. Look closely at where the ST segment starts in V2–V4.
Upsloping ST depression at the J point into tall, symmetrical T waves, plus ST elevation in aVR.
explanation: Upsloping ST depression of 1–3 mm at the J point in V2–V5, running into tall, symmetrical T waves, with slight ST elevation in aVR, in someone with ongoing chest pain. These de Winter T waves signal acute proximal LAD occlusion and are regarded as a STEMI equivalent, even with no ST elevation in the chest leads.
features: Upsloping ST depression at the J point, V2–V5
pearl: Tall T waves plus upsloping ST depression plus pain: think de Winter. Wellens, by contrast, appears once the pain has gone.

vignette: A 33-year-old woman, 20 weeks pregnant, has an ECG for occasional palpitations. This trace was recorded during one.
hints: Rate, rhythm, P waves, PR, QRS. Tick them off one by one.
Sometimes the answer is reassuringly boring.
explanation: Rate about 84/min, regular, an upright P wave before every QRS, PR about 160 ms, narrow QRS, normal ST-T: normal sinus rhythm. Resting heart rate rises by 10–20 beats/min in pregnancy and palpitations are common. A normal ECG captured during palpitations is reassuring.
features: Regular, with a P wave before every QRS
pearl: Read every ECG the same way: rate, rhythm, axis, intervals, morphology. A system beats a hunch.

vignette: A 74-year-old woman fainted at the shops. She is pale but alert. Lead II rhythm strip:
hints: Count the P waves against the QRS complexes.
Every second P wave is not followed by a QRS, and the PR of the conducted beats never changes.
explanation: Regular P waves at about 88/min, but only every second one is conducted, giving a ventricular rate of about 44/min. The conducted beats all have the same PR. With 2:1 block you can't see whether the PR would lengthen first, so you can't tell Mobitz I from Mobitz II on this strip alone.
features: Exactly two P waves per QRS
pearl: 2:1 block can't be labelled Mobitz I or II from one strip. A wide QRS or syncope makes an infranodal (Mobitz II-like) block more likely, so treat it as dangerous.

vignette: An 81-year-old man on the cardiology ward feels dizzy whenever he stands. Lead II rhythm strip:
hints: Some P waves do conduct, at a fixed PR.
Two P waves in a row are blocked before each conducted beat.
explanation: Regular P waves at about 96/min with a 3:1 pattern: two consecutive P waves blocked, then one conducted with a constant PR. Because some P waves still conduct with a fixed relationship, this is high-grade (advanced) AV block rather than complete heart block.
pearl: High-grade AV block (3:1 or worse) usually needs pacing. In complete heart block, P waves and QRS complexes are completely unrelated; here the conducted beats keep a fixed PR.

vignette: A 58-year-old man two hours after successful stenting for an anterior STEMI. The nurse notices this on the monitor. He feels fine; BP 124/76.
hints: Wide complexes, but count the rate.
Classically appears after the blocked artery has been reopened.
explanation: A regular wide-complex rhythm at about 80/min, with P waves marching through unrelated to the QRS. Too fast for an escape rhythm and too slow for VT: accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR), a classic reperfusion rhythm.
pearl: AIVR after reperfusion is usually benign and self-limiting. Don't shock it or suppress it with antiarrhythmics; the ventricles may be all that's keeping the rate up.

vignette: A 63-year-old man with heart failure has a routine monitor strip on the ward. Lead II:
hints: The wide beats come in pairs.
Three or more in a row would be called something else.
explanation: Sinus rhythm interrupted by pairs of consecutive wide, early ventricular complexes: ventricular couplets.
features: No P wave before the wide beats
pearl: Two PVCs in a row is a couplet; three or more at over 100/min is non-sustained VT. In heart failure, check potassium and magnesium and review the medicines.

vignette: A 29-year-old student feels her heart 'fluttering' after an all-nighter with energy drinks. Lead II rhythm strip:
hints: Every second beat comes early.
The early beats are narrow and have their own abnormal-looking P wave.
explanation: Every second beat is a premature narrow QRS preceded by an abnormal (inverted) P wave: a premature atrial complex after each sinus beat, called atrial bigeminy.
features: Alternating sinus beat and early beat
Early beats are narrow with an abnormal P wave
pearl: Atrial ectopics are common and usually benign; caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, stress and sleep deprivation are classic triggers. Narrow early beats point to an atrial origin, wide ones to a ventricular origin.

vignette: An 84-year-old man on digoxin and a beta blocker for atrial fibrillation feels tired and light-headed. Lead II rhythm strip:
answer: Atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response
options: Atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response
hints: Are there any P waves?
The gaps are irregular and long. Think about his medicines.
explanation: No P waves, an irregular baseline and an irregularly irregular ventricular rate of about 45/min: atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response, likely from too much rate-slowing medicine.
pearl: Slow AF in an older person on rate-control drugs: check digoxin levels, kidney function and potassium. Regular slow beats in AF suggest complete heart block with an escape rhythm.

vignette: A 66-year-old woman on digoxin, recovering from cardiac surgery. Lead II rhythm strip:
hints: The QRS is narrow, but look just after it.
Too fast to be an escape rhythm, too slow to be a tachycardia.
explanation: A regular narrow-complex rhythm at about 86/min with no P wave before the QRS and an inverted (retrograde) P wave just after it: an accelerated junctional rhythm (60–100/min).
features: No P wave before the QRS
Retrograde P wave after the QRS
pearl: Junctional escape is 40–60/min; accelerated junctional rhythm 60–100; junctional tachycardia over 100. Think digoxin toxicity, myocarditis, cardiac surgery and ischaemia.

vignette: A 52-year-old woman with COPD has had a racing heart for a day. Lead II rhythm strip:
hints: There is a P wave before each QRS. Look at which way it points.
An inverted P wave in lead II means the impulse isn't starting in the sinus node.
explanation: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at about 160/min with a P wave before every QRS, but the P waves are inverted in lead II. The atria are being driven from a single ectopic focus low in the atrium: focal atrial tachycardia.
features: One P wave before each QRS
P wave inverted in lead II
pearl: Sinus P waves are always upright in lead II. One abnormal P shape means focal atrial tachycardia; three or more different P shapes at over 100/min means multifocal atrial tachycardia.

vignette: A fit 35-year-old woman has an ECG before surgery. She has no symptoms. Lead II rhythm strip:
hints: The rate is normal and every beat has a P wave.
But the P waves point the wrong way in lead II, with a shortish PR.
explanation: A regular rhythm at about 64/min with a P wave before every QRS, but the P waves are inverted in lead II and the PR is short. The pacemaker is an ectopic focus low in the atrium: an ectopic (low) atrial rhythm.
features: Inverted P waves in lead II
pearl: Ectopic atrial rhythm is usually benign in a healthy person. The same P-wave pattern at over 100/min would be focal atrial tachycardia; without P waves before the QRS, think junctional.

vignette: An 88-year-old man collapses on the ward. No pulse. The monitor shows:
hints: The atria are still working.
Nothing is reaching the ventricles at all.
explanation: Regular P waves at about 70/min but no QRS complexes at all: the atria are depolarising, but nothing conducts and no escape rhythm has appeared. This is P-wave asystole (ventricular standstill), a non-shockable cardiac arrest.
pearl: Ventricular standstill is treated as asystole (CPR, adrenaline), but the P waves mean pacing may work, so consider it early. It can follow complete heart block when the escape rhythm fails.

vignette: A 67-year-old woman is in cardiac arrest. Leads are checked and the gain is turned up. The monitor shows:
hints: There's nothing organised here at all.
Always check the leads and the gain before calling it.
explanation: A nearly flat line with only slight baseline wander and noise: no P waves, no QRS complexes, no fibrillatory activity. With leads connected and gain checked, this is asystole.
pearl: Asystole is non-shockable: start CPR, give adrenaline and look for reversible causes (the 4 Hs and 4 Ts). A perfectly flat line is often a disconnected lead, so check the patient and the leads.

vignette: A 77-year-old man with Parkinson's disease has a routine ECG before a hip operation. He is chatting comfortably. Lead II rhythm strip:
hints: Look past the fuzzy baseline: are the QRS complexes regular?
The patient is talking to you, and the wobble is about 5–6 per second.
explanation: Regular, normal QRS complexes at about 72/min hidden in a busy, jittery baseline. The underlying rhythm is sinus: the baseline noise is tremor artefact, not an arrhythmia.
features: Regular QRS complexes at a normal rate
pearl: Treat the patient, not the monitor. Parkinsonian tremor, shivering and patient movement can mimic flutter, AF or even VF. Ask the patient to relax and repeat the trace.

vignette: A 69-year-old man on a beta blocker has a routine ECG at the GP. He feels well. Lead II rhythm strip:
hints: Look at the baseline between the QRS complexes.
Count the sawtooth waves for each QRS.
explanation: A regular sawtooth baseline at about 300/min with four flutter waves for every QRS, giving a regular ventricular rate of about 75/min: atrial flutter with 4:1 block.
pearl: Atrial flutter carries a stroke risk like AF, so it needs the same anticoagulation assessment. Typical flutter is very treatable with catheter ablation.

vignette: A 22-year-old athlete has a screening ECG. He has no symptoms. Lead II rhythm strip:
hints: Every QRS has a P wave, but they don't all look the same.
The rate is under 100.
explanation: A slightly irregular rhythm at about 70/min. Every QRS has a P wave, but the P waves vary in shape (at least three different shapes) with varying PR intervals: wandering atrial pacemaker.
features: Three or more different P-wave shapes
pearl: Same pattern, different rate: under 100/min it's wandering atrial pacemaker (often benign, e.g. in athletes); over 100/min it's multifocal atrial tachycardia (often severe lung disease).

vignette: A 49-year-old man collapses in a gym. A bystander attaches an AED and the screen shows:
hints: You can't separate the QRS from the T wave.
Regular, very fast, sine-wave-like.
explanation: A very rapid (about 280/min), regular, sine-wave-like wide-complex rhythm where QRS and T waves merge: ventricular flutter, which usually degenerates into VF.
pearl: Ventricular flutter is treated like VF: it's shockable and pulseless. Torsades twists around the baseline; VF is chaotic with no regular pattern.

vignette: An 82-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation takes digoxin. Her ECG at a routine check:
hints: Look at the shape of the ST depression, not just its depth.
Think of a reverse tick, and check her medicine list.
explanation: AF at a controlled rate with sagging, 'reverse tick' (scooped) ST depression in the inferior and lateral leads, flattened T waves and a short QT: digoxin effect.
pearl: Digoxin effect is expected at therapeutic levels and isn't toxicity. Toxicity shows as new arrhythmias (bidirectional VT, atrial tachycardia with block, bradycardia) plus nausea and visual changes.

vignette: A 61-year-old woman with breast cancer has bone pain, constipation and confusion. ECG:
hints: Measure from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave.
The ST segment has almost disappeared. Think bones, stones, groans and moans.
explanation: Sinus rhythm with a short QT interval: the T wave starts almost straight after the QRS, with very little ST segment. In this story (cancer, bone pain, constipation, confusion) that means hypercalcaemia.
features: T wave starts right after the QRS
pearl: High calcium shortens the QT and low calcium lengthens it (by stretching the ST segment). Malignancy and primary hyperparathyroidism cause most hypercalcaemia.

vignette: A 47-year-old woman, three days after thyroid surgery, has tingling around her mouth and cramps in her hands. ECG:
hints: Measure the QT, then look at which part is long.
The T wave itself is normal: it's the flat segment before it that's stretched.
explanation: Sinus rhythm with a prolonged QT, caused by a long, flat ST segment with a normal-looking T wave at the end. After thyroid surgery with perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm, this is hypocalcaemia (often from parathyroid damage).
pearl: In hypocalcaemia the ST segment stretches; in congenital long QT and with QT-prolonging drugs the T wave itself is broad or notched. Check Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs.

vignette: A 79-year-old woman had a brief faint while gardening. Her ECG:
hints: The QRS is wide with an RSR' in V1.
Now check the axis: it's swung far to the left.
explanation: A wide QRS with an RSR' pattern in V1 and a wide S wave in I and V6 (right bundle branch block), plus left axis deviation with rS in the inferior leads (left anterior fascicular block): bifascicular block.
features: RBBB: RSR' in V1, wide S in I and V6
pearl: Bifascicular block plus unexplained syncope warrants investigation for intermittent complete heart block (Holter, or a loop recorder if needed). Only one fascicle is left working.

vignette: A slim 55-year-old man with no lung or heart disease has an ECG before surgery. Echo was normal.
hints: Lead I is mostly negative and lead III tall: which way is the axis?
The QRS is narrow and the echo shows no right ventricular cause.
explanation: Narrow QRS with right axis deviation: rS in I and aVL and qR in II, III and aVF. With no right ventricular hypertrophy, lung disease or other cause, this is left posterior fascicular block.
features: qR in III and aVF, narrow QRS
pearl: LPFB is a diagnosis of exclusion: rule out RVH, PE, lateral MI and lead misplacement first. It's much rarer than LAFB because the posterior fascicle is thick and has a double blood supply.

vignette: A 41-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension is increasingly breathless on exertion.
hints: V1 has a dominant R wave. What can do that?
Right axis, tall R and T inversion in V1–V2, peaked P in II.
explanation: Right axis deviation, a dominant R wave in V1 with ST depression and T inversion in V1–V2 (right ventricular strain), deep S waves in V5–V6 and a tall peaked P wave in lead II: right ventricular hypertrophy with right atrial enlargement.
features: Dominant R in V1 with strain pattern
Deep S in V5–V6, P pulmonale
pearl: Causes of a dominant R in V1: RVH, RBBB, posterior MI, WPW (type A), dextrocardia, HCM and normal in young children. The clinical story usually separates them.

vignette: A 26-year-old man has his first ECG at a sports medical. The nurse checks the leads and they're placed correctly.
hints: Lead I is completely upside down: P, QRS and T.
The leads are on correctly. Now look at how the R waves change across V1 to V6.
explanation: Lead I is globally inverted (negative P, QRS and T), aVR is upright, and the R waves get smaller from V1 to V6 instead of bigger. With leads correctly placed, the heart is on the right: dextrocardia.
features: Inverted P, QRS and T in lead I
pearl: Swapped arm leads also invert lead I, but the chest leads stay normal. In dextrocardia the chest leads lose R waves across V1–V6; repeat the ECG with right-sided chest leads. Think of Kartagener syndrome.

vignette: A 58-year-old woman's routine ECG looks odd compared with last year's, which was normal. She feels well.
hints: Lead I is completely upside down: P, QRS and T.
Now compare the chest leads with that. Do they look normal?
explanation: Lead I is globally inverted and aVR is upright, but the chest leads show normal R-wave progression from V1 to V6. That combination means the left and right arm electrodes have been swapped, not that the heart has moved.
features: Inverted P, QRS and T in lead I
pearl: The commonest ECG 'abnormality' is a misplaced electrode. If lead I is upside down but V1–V6 look normal, re-check the arm leads before diagnosing anything.

vignette: A 44-year-old woman with lung cancer has worsening breathlessness and a raised JVP. BP 92/70, HR 112.
hints: The complexes are small. Now compare each beat with the next.
The heart is swinging back and forth inside a fluid-filled sac.
explanation: Sinus tachycardia with low QRS voltages and beat-to-beat variation in QRS height (electrical alternans). With hypotension, a raised JVP and cancer, this suggests a large pericardial effusion with tamponade.
features: QRS height alternates beat to beat
pearl: Electrical alternans is specific for a large effusion, as the heart swings within it. Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis: hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad). Get an urgent echo.

vignette: A fit 24-year-old Black man has an ECG at a cardiology clinic after his brother's routine screen. He feels well.
hints: The ST segments are raised, but look at their shape and the notch at the J point.
Young, fit, symptom-free, with no reciprocal changes.
explanation: Mild concave ST elevation in V2–V5 with notched J points ('fish hooks'), tall T waves and a slow sinus rate, in a fit young man without symptoms and without reciprocal ST depression: benign early repolarisation.
features: No reciprocal ST depression, slow sinus rate
pearl: Early repolarisation is common in young men, athletes and people of African descent. Pericarditis has widespread ST elevation with PR depression; STEMI has convex ST elevation and reciprocal changes. If unsure, compare with old ECGs and repeat.

vignette: A 72-year-old man has crushing chest pain and is sweaty. BP 98/60.
answer: ST elevation in aVR with widespread ST depression
options: ST elevation in aVR with widespread ST depression
hints: Don't ignore aVR.
Widespread ST depression plus one lead going the other way.
explanation: Widespread ST depression in I, II and V3–V6 with ST elevation in aVR in a patient with ongoing chest pain: a pattern of diffuse subendocardial ischaemia, raising concern for left main or severe three-vessel coronary disease.
features: Widespread ST depression (six or more leads)
pearl: This pattern isn't a STEMI by the usual criteria, but with ongoing pain and instability it needs urgent cardiology input and angiography. Other causes include severe anaemia, tachyarrhythmia and aortic dissection.

vignette: A 55-year-old man arrives 20 minutes after sudden, severe central chest pain began.
hints: The T waves in V2–V4 are huge. Are they narrow and peaked, or broad-based?
Twenty minutes into the pain, the ST segments haven't caught up yet.
explanation: Tall, broad-based, symmetrical T waves in V2–V4 out of proportion to the QRS, with only slight ST elevation, 20 minutes into ischaemic pain: hyperacute T waves, the earliest sign of an anterior STEMI.
features: Broad, tall, symmetrical T waves V2–V4
pearl: Hyperacute T waves are broad-based and bulky; hyperkalaemic T waves are narrow and tented. Repeat the ECG every 10–15 minutes. Evolving STEMI changes fast.

vignette: A 67-year-old man had a large anterior heart attack six months ago. Now breathless with ankle swelling; no chest pain today. Troponin normal.
hints: Q waves have already formed, and the T waves are small.
The ST elevation hasn't settled months after the infarct.
explanation: Deep QS waves in V1–V3 and a Q in V4 with persistent ST elevation and small T waves, months after an anterior MI, with no new pain and a normal troponin: left ventricular aneurysm.
features: Persistent ST elevation with small T waves
Months after an MI, troponin normal
pearl: Persistent ST elevation after an old MI suggests an aneurysm. Small T waves relative to the QRS favour aneurysm; big T waves favour acute STEMI. Echo confirms it. Watch for heart failure, thrombus and VT.

vignette: A 70-year-old woman sees a new GP and brings her old letters: she had a heart attack in 2019. No symptoms today.
hints: Look at the start of the QRS in II, III and aVF.
The ST segments are flat: this isn't happening now.
explanation: Pathological Q waves in II, III and aVF with isoelectric ST segments and upright T waves: an old (established) inferior myocardial infarction.
features: Pathological Q waves in II, III, aVF
pearl: Pathological Q waves are over 40 ms wide or over 25% of the R-wave height, in two contiguous leads. A small isolated Q in lead III alone can be normal.

vignette: An 80-year-old man with known left bundle branch block has had crushing chest pain for 40 minutes.
hints: In LBBB, the ST segment normally goes the opposite way to the QRS.
Here, in leads with a positive QRS, the ST goes up too.
explanation: Left bundle branch block, but with concordant ST elevation (in the same direction as the QRS) in I, V5 and V6. In LBBB the ST normally goes against the QRS, so concordant elevation meets a Sgarbossa criterion: acute MI.
features: LBBB morphology (broad QRS, deep S in V1)
Concordant ST elevation in leads with a positive QRS
pearl: Sgarbossa criteria (concordant ST elevation 1 mm or more, concordant ST depression in V1–V3, or excessively discordant ST elevation) help find MI hidden by LBBB. A new LBBB alone is no longer treated as a STEMI equivalent.

vignette: A 38-year-old man of Japanese descent has an ECG at an insurance medical. His echo later shows a thick heart apex.
hints: Tall voltages, and look at the depth of those T waves.
Very deep, symmetrical T inversion in the chest leads, in a well person with a thick apex.
explanation: Very tall QRS voltages with giant, symmetrical T-wave inversion in V3–V5 in a symptom-free person: the classic pattern of apical hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Yamaguchi syndrome), confirmed by the thickened apex on echo.
pearl: Apical HCM is more common in people of East Asian descent. Giant T inversion can also mean Wellens or cerebral T waves, so put it with the story and image the heart (echo or MRI).

vignette: A 23-year-old woman, a keen distance runner, fainted during a race. Her uncle died suddenly at 30.
hints: Look closely just after the QRS in V1 and V2.
T inversion beyond V1 in an adult, exercise-related syncope, and a family history of sudden death.
explanation: T-wave inversion in V1–V3 and a small notch at the very end of the QRS in V1–V2 (an epsilon wave), in a young athlete with exertional syncope and a family history of sudden death: arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC).
features: Epsilon wave after the QRS in V1–V2
pearl: ARVC is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes, and endurance exercise speeds it up. Refer urgently: cardiac MRI, Holter, genetic testing and family screening.

vignette: A 27-year-old woman is drowsy after an overdose of her antidepressant tablets, taken an hour ago. HR 126.
hints: The QRS is wide. Check aVR carefully.
Sodium channel blockade from her tablets.
explanation: Sinus tachycardia with a widened QRS (about 140 ms), a tall terminal R wave in aVR and a deep terminal S in I: sodium channel blockade from tricyclic antidepressant overdose.
features: Terminal R wave in aVR over 3 mm
pearl: A QRS over 100 ms predicts seizures and over 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmias. The antidote for sodium channel blockade is IV sodium bicarbonate. Call your poisons centre.

vignette: A 19-year-old man with palpitations is pale and clammy. HR about 190, BP 94/58.
options: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
hints: Is it regular? Is it narrow?
Fast, irregular and broad: the impulses are taking a shortcut that bypasses the AV node.
explanation: A very fast, irregularly irregular, broad-complex tachycardia (about 190/min) with slurred delta-wave upstrokes: atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.
pearl: Never give AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta blockers, digoxin) in pre-excited AF: they can push it into VF. If unstable, synchronised DC cardioversion; if stable, procainamide or flecainide, then ablation.

vignette: A 31-year-old man of Thai background had a febrile illness and fainted. His brother died in his sleep at 35.
hints: Look at the shape of the ST segment in V2.
It dips between two humps, then the T wave is upright.
explanation: In V1–V2, a terminal r' followed by ST elevation with a 'saddleback' shape (the ST dips then rises into an upright T wave): Brugada type 2 pattern. With syncope and a family history of sudden death, it needs specialist assessment.
pearl: Only the coved type 1 pattern is diagnostic. A type 2 pattern can be unmasked into type 1 by fever or a drug challenge (ajmaline/flecainide) under specialist care. Brugada is more common in men of Southeast Asian descent.

vignette: A 57-year-old woman who had rheumatic fever as a child in Fiji is breathless on exertion. An echo shows a narrowed mitral valve.
hints: The QRS and T are fine. Zoom in on the P waves.
Broad and double-humped in II, with a big negative tail in V1.
explanation: Sinus rhythm with broad (over 120 ms), notched, double-humped P waves in lead II and a deep, wide negative terminal P wave in V1: left atrial enlargement (P mitrale), here from rheumatic mitral stenosis.
features: Broad, notched P wave in II (over 120 ms)
Deep negative terminal P in V1
pearl: Rheumatic heart disease is still common in many low- and middle-income countries and in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and Pacific Islander communities. Mitral stenosis enlarges the left atrium, which often leads to AF.

vignette: A 66-year-old man with long-standing severe COPD has worsening breathlessness.
hints: The QRS and T are fine. Look at the P waves.
Tall and pointed in the inferior leads.
explanation: Sinus rhythm with tall, peaked P waves (over 2.5 mm) in II, III and aVF: right atrial enlargement (P pulmonale), from chronic lung disease and pulmonary hypertension.
features: Tall, peaked P waves (over 2.5 mm) in II
pearl: Tall peaked P = right atrium (P pulmonale); broad notched P = left atrium (P mitrale). Peaked T waves, not P waves, are the hyperkalaemia sign.

vignette: A 71-year-old woman has had palpitations and breathlessness since this morning. BP 118/70. Lead II rhythm strip:
answer: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
options: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
hints: Measure the gaps between beats. Are any two the same?
No P waves, just a wobbly baseline.
explanation: An irregularly irregular narrow-complex tachycardia at about 150/min with no P waves and a chaotic, fibrillating baseline: atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response.
pearl: Control the rate, look for the trigger (infection, alcohol, thyroid, ischaemia) and assess stroke risk with CHA2DS2-VA. A regular rate fixed at 150 suggests flutter instead.
